articles.headline: "He Hath Bitten off More than he Can Chew."
articles.text:
The two following articles appeared in the Bismarck Tribune of Sunday.

"Sheriff Willard of Medora, arrived from the west yesterday."

"The fact that Editor Packard has taken a stand against the stockmen and in favor of Meyers, who was recently brought back for stealing cattle by Sheriff Willard, has prompted some of Mr. Packard's acquaintances to lose confidence in him as that lofty champion of justice he declared himself when he entered upon his journalistic career in the Bad Lands."

The above articles fit together so well that "'Twere a sin to part them" and we publish them in full.

Up to this time we never have and probably never will again, allow a controversy, personal to ourselves, to appear in the columns of a paper that we own. In this case, however, Mr. Willard has found such ready mouth-pieces in other papers, that for two reasons we allow ourselves a personal explanation; 1st., because he has allowed his causeless spite toward us to lead him to indirectly charge a perfectly innocent man with stealing cattle and, 2nd., to show our exact position in this matter and the justice of our previous remarks, which caused the above article. To mutual acquaintances, we are perfectly willing to rest the case without argument.

The last article quoted from the Tribune states that we have arrayed ourselves against the sentiment of the stockmen in believing Myers to be innocent. It further states that we set up a lofty standard of justice when we came to the Bad Lands. As Mr. Willard has mixed his dates somewhat on the latter charge and confused the time we first came here with the time when he told us, when he was running for sheriff and our name was dragged before the public against our will as justice of the peace, that "There's plenty of money in it if the justice of the peace and the sheriff stand in," we can pass that by as an inadvertance on his part.

The gist of the article charges that George Myers is guilty of stealing cattle and that the stockmen here join in the charge.

To make the matter perfectly clear, we will again state the history of the case, with some additional points over our last account.

George Myers is now and for several years has been working for the Maltese Cross outfit, of which Ferris & Merrifield are managers and Theodore Roosevelt of New York is proprietor. Instead of spending every cent he earned in extravagance, he has constantly turned the greater share of his wages into cattle and horses. In this way he bought a bunch of cattle of Ferris & Merrifield, but before they were all branded, two escaped. During the beef round-up, these two animals were found on the Maltese Cross range and were turned over to Myers by Sylvanus Ferris, one of the managers, in the presence of the representatives of at least two other outfits. Whether they were the identical two animals in question, does not make a particle of difference. They were mavericks (unbranded cattle) and as such, according to a by-law of the Little Missouri River Stockgrowers' Association, belonged to the range on which they were found. This reduces it to a personal matter between Ferris & Merrifield and Myers. They settled the business satisfactorily to themselves and it is no one's else business. There was no sign of disagreement by the representatives of other brands present and the matter was a virtual bill of sale by Ferris & Merrifield to Myers.

The two animals were then driven with the Maltese Cross beef cattle to Dickinson, to be shipped to market. To identify and hold them, they had been thrown and Myers' brand cut in the hair with a knife. This was done with the assistance of the representatives of two other brands.

Mr. Willard, in his capacity as inspector for the Montana Stockgrowers' Association, inspected these cattle while being loaded at Dickinson. He either noticed these two cattle or he did not. If he did not, then is he indeed a poor inspector not to tell the difference between a regular Maltese Cross brand and a 44—hair brand. If he did notice the two cattle, why did he not report them at the time, unless it was that he wished to make up in mileage, the expenses of a pleasure trip which he took to Joliet, Ill., while on his way to arrest Myers? This is also a question for our tax-payers to answer when they go down into their pockets for the $1,500 or $2,000 this suit is likely to cost.

Up to date, the above are the facts in the case, and they absolutely and beyond all question, prove that George is innocent.

The article quoted states that the stockmen on the river believe in George's guilt. At the time we wrote our previous article, we had not spoken with a solitary stockman, nor did we know the opinion of one of them. We knew the facts in the case and we also knew that George Myers was not a fool. He would have been a fool in the worst sense, if he had for the value of two animals, lost the respect and esteem which he has gained by his honest, manly conduct, not only here, but at his old home in Ohio, where he could have gotten bail for $200,000 had it been necessary. Since our last issue, we have spoken with several stockmen and they fairly scont the idea of George's guilt. We think we are within bounds when we state that there is not a solitary man, stockman or otherwise, in this country or any where else, who knows the facts in the case who will for a moment believe George guilty. The whole course of his life is utterly against any such assumption.
articles.summary: Packard answers Bismarck Tribune items attacking him for defending George Myers, a Maltese Cross hand accused of stealing two cattle, sets out how Sylvane Ferris turned the mavericks over to Myers, and accuses Sheriff Willard of spite and padding his mileage.

articles.text: The tax case of Billings Co's tax-payers against Stark Co., resisting the payment of taxes, came up last Friday before Judge Francis at Bismarck. T. R. Selmes appeared for Billings county and Mr. Flannery for Stark county. The whole day was consumed in the argument. Judge Francis rendered a pro forma decision that the preliminary injunction should be dissolved, as the attorneys have made an agreed case that no steps shall be taken toward collecting the taxes until the matter is decided by the supreme court. This will be done some time in February. Meantime the matter is virtually as it was, except that Billings county's case seems to be growing stronger. The only similar case that has hitherto been decided for the ground against which we are fighting was decided so simply on the question of expediency. Other decisions favor our side. The case is assuming a far wider scope than was first expected and will bring up prominently the gross earnings railroad law. Mr. Bullitt of St. Paul, is associate counsel with Mr. Selmes and has prepared a voluminous brief which almost goes back before the flood in proving our position to be good.
articles.summary: The Billings County taxpayers' suit against Stark County was argued before Judge Francis at Bismarck and sent on an agreed case to the territorial supreme court.

articles.headline: A Mistake Brand Adopted.
articles.text:
ST. JOSEPH, Nov. 20, 1886.

EDITOR HERALD.—The Executive committee of the Apache County Stock Growers Association, recognizing the necessity for a distinguishing mark or brand, for using in returning calves, branded through mistake and where the owners do not care to vent their brand, have adopted the following as a mistake brand."

In case where a calf has been branded by mistake; both the first calf and the one giving in return should have M put on the right side of the animals neck.

This will prevent in a measure those annoying disputes over such cases and show both parties interested whether, or not, a calf branded through error has been returned.

The "mistake brand" has been found of great use in all range countries, and the Committee hope it will be used by all Association members, and that each will endeavor to have its use made general by all his neighbors.

The brand has been recorded, and is the property of the Association. By order of the Executive Committee.

WILL C. BARNES, Sec.
articles.summary: Reprinted letter from the Apache County Stock Growers Association announcing an "M" mistake brand for returned calves.

articles.text: A series of chances [changes?] has put Billings county to some straits for enough officers to transact county business. At present, but two of the commissioners have qualified and one of them is in Texas on business. W. F. Van Driesche was elected treasurer, but resigned and J. C. Fisher was appointed in his stead. But Mr. Fisher is on a six week's visit in Elyria, Ohio. No justice of the peace has as yet qualified and the terms of the old ones expire Jan. 1. It behooves Mr. Rowe, the third commissioner, to qualify at once and rescue us from our present "slough of despond."
articles.summary: Billings County is short of qualified officers: one commissioner is in Texas, the new treasurer is in Ohio, and no justice of the peace has qualified.

articles.headline: The Live Stock Commissioners.
articles.text:
The Illinois State Board of Live Stock Commissioners have had most serious work in charge for the past few months. Their service during seasons of reputed cattle plague in the State are onerous in the extreme, and their labors very exacting and extended in almost any event. In view of the gravity of the situation, as considered by cattle-growers here and elsewhere throughout the United States, any formal utterances of the Live Stock Commission will command attention. This board met in Chicago yesterday, and their annual report will be made to Governor Oglesby to-day.

It is stated in the United States census of 1880 that the following was the number of live stock in Illinois then:

Horses, 1,023,082; Mules and asses, 123,278; Working oxen, 3,346; Milch cows, 869,913; Other cattle, 1,515,063; Sheep, 1,037,073; Swine, 5,170,266.

The more careful authorities will admit that the addition generally of 10 per cent, to these figures will be a very moderate rate of increase for the past six years. Upon such returns it is perfectly safe to place the value of the live stock interests of Illinois at not less than $100,000,000, or fully one-fifth of the assessed personal property of the State. The vast stock interest grouped about Chicago is scarcely to be computed. The remark made by a conservative man whose specialty was a line of high thoroughbreds may be taken as illustrative of what is involved in a cattle disease like that which has been under investigation and treatment here during the past three months. He estimated that the reputed disease and the quarantine placed upon Illinois cattle in consequence had in three months resulted in the loss of over $1,000,000 to his line of cattle alone.

Two years ago the General Assembly appropriated $50,000 for paying for slaughtered animals not diseased, which had to be killed to prevent the disease from spreading. The sum of $30,000 was appropriated for the purpose of meeting the necessary expenses of the commission, such as traveling expenses, hotels, the services of the veterinarian, etc.; that to say, $25,000 a year for paying for slaughtered animals, and $5,000 a year for the running of the office, etc. In Chicago alone there have been about 3,000 animals placed in quarantine. The distillery-fed cattle in Chicago are reported at 6,000. The city of Peoria has in its distilleries about 10,000. The utmost care was necessary to keep the infected or exposed cattle, away from other cattle, and to prevent the spread of the disease.

It may be asked how it affects Illinois that so many precautions are necessary, and why these precautions are necessary at all. It is the minimum cost that the State of Illinois appropriates $30,000 a year, and then only on great pressure, to protect property valued at the lowest possible estimate at $100,000,000. But this is not all. It is estimated that Chicago's sales of cattle bought here every fall, to be taken to Springfield, Ill., and there distributed to the farms of their purchasers in neighboring counties this year, fell off about 6,000 in consequence of the reported cattle disease in this city. That was a result, too, experienced in the State itself. The disastrous effects are still more widely extended. The States of Michigan and Iowa, for example, have publicly declared against and will not permit the importation of any Illinois cattle across their borders until it is clearly known and officially stated by the Illinois Live Stock Commissioners and other high, competent authority that the dread disease is effectually stamped out. The loss to a single strain of cattle since September is estimated at $1,000,000, and the total loss can not be less than $5,000,000 or $6,000,000 for that period. It is not necessary to call attention to the effect of such diseases upon the money loaning circles of the community, and how timid financial institutions become in such a presence.

The Live Stock Commissioners will have expended all their appropriation by the end of this year. The unusual outlay incident to the outbreak here this fall has exhausted the amount set apart by the Legislature for this purpose. It is understood that the commission will ask for an appropriation of not less than $200,000 to meet all the exigencies which may arise during the next two years. If the principal on which the work is based be correct, and that is admitted, the amount is desired should not be matter for serious dispute. If any sum is needed at all, it is likely to be a large sum. The reluctance of those having diseased cattle to report them arises from the fact that they can not collect from the State anything if such diseased animals are killed. A larger and broader policy will have to be inaugurated. The State must not endeavor to put a premium on dishonesty or the secreting of infected cattle, but rather make it an object for persons owning diseased cattle to report the facts as soon as they discovered the danger.—[Inter Ocean.
articles.summary: Reprint from the Chicago Inter Ocean on the Illinois Live Stock Commissioners, the cattle-disease quarantine around Chicago and its costs.

articles.headline: Commissioners' Meeting.
articles.text:
A special meeting of the board of county commissioners of Billings' county, was held at the usual place of meeting on Dec. 2, 1886.

Meeting was called to order by the chairman of the board.

Present: Commissioners Truscott and Goodall and Clerk Williamson.

County Treasurer W. F. Van Driesche's resignation being on file, the object of the meeting was to examine his resignation and if approved, to appoint a new treasurer.

On motion, the resignation was accepted and J. C. Fisher appointed county treasurer for the year 1887.

On motion, Fisher's bond of $4,000, to the county of Billings, was approved.

On motion, the board adjourned.

J. C. WILLIAMSON,
County Clerk.
articles.summary: Billings County commissioners accepted Van Driesche's resignation as treasurer and appointed J. C. Fisher.

Brand: Bad Lands Cattle Co., M. Wadsworth, Manager, P.O. Medora — Pd and others; range Little Missouri river fifteen miles north of Medora
Brand: Towers & Gudgell, P.O. Keith, Montana — OX; range south of N.P.R.R. on Little Missouri river and Beaver creek
articles.summary: Directory of page 4 display advertisers and cattle and horse brand notices, including Theodore Roosevelt's Chimney Butte Ranch (Maltese Cross) brand.

events.date_basis: Bismarck Tribune "of Sunday" before Thu 23 Dec 1886
events.title: Bismarck Tribune attacks Packard over the Myers cattle case
events.summary: The Bismarck Tribune printed that Editor Packard had taken a stand against the stockmen in favor of George Myers, whom Sheriff Willard had brought back on a cattle-stealing charge. Packard reprinted both items and replied at length.
events.excerpt: "The fact that Editor Packard has taken a stand against the stockmen and in favor of Meyers, who was recently brought back for stealing cattle by Sheriff Willard"

events.date_basis: Tribune of Sunday 19 Dec says "yesterday"
events.title: Sheriff Willard arrives in Bismarck from the west
events.summary: The Bismarck Tribune, as quoted, reported Sheriff Willard of Medora arrived from the west the day before.
events.excerpt: "Sheriff Willard of Medora, arrived from the west yesterday."

events.date_basis: "During the beef round-up" of 1886; exact date not given
events.title: Sylvane Ferris turns two mavericks over to Maltese Cross hand George Myers
events.summary: Packard reported that George Myers, a hand on Theodore Roosevelt's Maltese Cross outfit, had bought cattle from Ferris & Merrifield; two strays found on the Maltese Cross range during the beef round-up were turned over to him by Sylvanus Ferris before witnesses from two other outfits.
events.excerpt: "these two animals were found on the Maltese Cross range and were turned over to Myers by Sylvanus Ferris, one of the managers"

events.date_basis: Packard's defense of George Myers, issue of Thu 23 Dec 1886
events.title: Cow Boy defends George Myers against cattle-theft charge
events.summary: Packard argued that Myers, who has worked several years for the Maltese Cross outfit owned by Theodore Roosevelt, is innocent, that the stockmen he has since spoken with scout the charge, and that the suit may cost Billings County taxpayers $1,500 or $2,000. He also accused Willard of a pleasure trip to Joliet, Ill., on the way to arrest Myers.
events.excerpt: "George Myers is now and for several years has been working for the Maltese Cross outfit, of which Ferris & Merrifield are managers and Theodore Roosevelt of New York is proprietor."

events.date_basis: "is now traveling" in issue of Thu 23 Dec 1886
events.title: Theodore Roosevelt traveling in Europe with his bride
events.summary: The Cow Boy reported that Theodore Roosevelt was traveling in Europe with his bride and said his trip would be shortened by his coming to Medora to prove George Myers owned the two cattle.
events.excerpt: "Theodore Roosevelt is now traveling in Europe with his bride. His trip will be materially shortened by his coming here"

events.date_basis: Reported in issue of Thu 23 Dec 1886; date of issue not given
events.title: Warrants issued for Henry Williams and Jack Tisdale in Myers case
events.summary: Warrants were issued for the arrest of Henry Williams and Jack Tisdale as accessories in the case against George Myers; Williams was under bail.
events.excerpt: "Warrants have been issued for the arrest of Henry Williams and Jack Tisdale as accessories in the case against George Myers."

events.date_basis: "last Friday" before Thu 23 Dec 1886
events.title: Billings County tax case argued before Judge Francis at Bismarck
events.summary: The Billings County taxpayers' case against Stark County was argued all day; Judge Francis dissolved the preliminary injunction pro forma on an agreed case to go to the supreme court, with T. R. Selmes and Mr. Bullitt of St. Paul for Billings County.
events.excerpt: "Judge Francis rendered a pro forma decision that the preliminary injunction should be dissolved"

events.date_basis: "some time in February" from issue of Thu 23 Dec 1886
events.title: Territorial supreme court expected to decide Billings–Stark tax case
events.summary: The supreme court was expected to decide the Billings County tax case some time in February.
events.excerpt: "This will be done some time in February."

events.date_basis: "last Friday" before Thu 23 Dec 1886; left camp "on the 10th"
events.title: Mike Seitz reaches Mandan with Capt. Cotton's horses
events.summary: Mike Seitz, who left the Logging Camp on December 10 with two of Capt. Cotton's horses, arrived in Mandan after a hard trip, making only ten miles the last day.
events.excerpt: "arrived in Mandan last Friday. The trip was a hard one, he only making ten miles the last day."

events.date_basis: Reported in issue of Thu 23 Dec 1886
events.title: Northern Pacific cuts Dakota fares to four cents a mile
events.summary: The Northern Pacific reduced all passenger fares in Dakota to a uniform four cents a mile.
events.excerpt: "The Northern Pacific has reduced all passenger fares in Dakota to a uniform rate of four cents a mile."

events.date_basis: Reported in issue of Thu 23 Dec 1886
events.title: Heavy holiday express traffic between Helena and Medora
events.summary: Express messengers were hard at work with holiday presents; one carried 201 way-bills between Helena and Medora.
events.excerpt: "One of them had 201 way-bills between Helena and Medora."

events.date_basis: Dated in the minutes
events.title: Billings County commissioners appoint J. C. Fisher treasurer
events.summary: At a special meeting, Commissioners Truscott and Goodall accepted W. F. Van Driesche's resignation as county treasurer, appointed J. C. Fisher treasurer for 1887 and approved his $4,000 bond.
events.excerpt: "the resignation was accepted and J. C. Fisher appointed county treasurer for the year 1887."

events.date_basis: Reported in issue of Thu 23 Dec 1886
events.title: Billings County short of qualified officers
events.summary: The Cow Boy reported only two commissioners had qualified, one of them away in Texas, that new treasurer J. C. Fisher was on a six weeks' visit to Elyria, Ohio, and that no justice of the peace had qualified before the old terms expired Jan. 1; it urged commissioner Rowe to qualify.
events.excerpt: "It behooves Mr. Rowe, the third commissioner, to qualify at once and rescue us from our present \"slough of despond.\""

events.date_basis: "last week" before Thu 23 Dec 1886
events.title: Alex. McKenzie of Bismarck visits Medora
events.summary: Alex. McKenzie of Bismarck spent several days in Medora.
events.excerpt: "Alex. McKenzie of Bismarck spent several days in Medora last week."

events.date_basis: "Tuesday morning" before Thu 23 Dec 1886
events.title: Mrs. James Foley and daughters return to Bismarck
events.summary: Mrs. James Foley and two daughters returned to Bismarck.
events.excerpt: "Mrs. James Foley and two daughters returned to Bismarck Tuesday morning."

events.date_basis: Reported in issue of Thu 23 Dec 1886
events.title: John Norris opens restaurant in Coleman's building
events.summary: John Norris, formerly cook for Gill Kennedy, opened a restaurant in M. M. Coleman's building.
events.excerpt: "has opened a restaurant in M. M. Coleman's building."

events.date_basis: Reported in issue of Thu 23 Dec 1886
events.title: Chas. S. Eaton and family go to Mandan for the winter
events.summary: Chas. S. Eaton, his wife and his wife's mother went to Mandan for the winter and set up housekeeping.
events.excerpt: "will spend the winter in Mandn. They have already gone to housekeeping."

events.date_basis: "lately" in issue of Thu 23 Dec 1886
events.title: Overflow on river ice makes Little Missouri crossings nearly impassable
events.summary: Travelers using the river as a highway had difficulty at the crossings, with two to three feet of water on the old ice downriver.
events.excerpt: "the water is between two and three feet deep on the old ice"

events.date_basis: "Monday night" before Thu 23 Dec 1886
events.title: Wrestling match at the Senate ends in a draw
events.summary: Jim Hayes and W. H. Wall wrestled at the Senate; each took a fall and the match was declared a draw.
events.excerpt: "A wrestling match came off at the Senate, Monday night, between Jim Hayes and W. H. Wall."

events.date_basis: "Christmas" after Thu 23 Dec 1886
events.title: Oyster-eating match for a silver cup planned for Christmas
events.summary: "Van" and "Nitch" were to eat an oyster match for a silver cup on Christmas, billed as the society event of the season.
events.excerpt: "\"Van\" and \"Nitch\" will eat an oyster match for a silver cup."

events.date_basis: Notice in issue of Thu 23 Dec 1886
events.title: Packard closes out his Studebaker wagon stock
events.summary: A. T. Packard offered his stock of Studebaker wagons below wholesale factory rates for cash to close out the stock on hand, and also offered wagon extras.
events.excerpt: "The only reason for making these rates is to close out stock on hand. They must and shall go soon."

events.date_basis: Reported in issue of Thu 23 Dec 1886
events.title: Max Sanford of Dickinson expands holiday stock
events.summary: Max Sanford of Dickinson added $400 of silverware and other holiday goods and took mail orders by postal card.
events.excerpt: "Sanford, of Dickinson, has been adding largely to his stock"

events.date_basis: Reported in issue of Thu 23 Dec 1886
events.title: Dr. Heber Roberts practising in Livingston
events.summary: Dr. Heber Roberts was reported practising in Livingston.
events.excerpt: "Dr. Heber Roberts is now practising in Livingston."
